title: Quantum entanglement
summary: See how two particles can stay linked at any distance, and why that link still can't send a message.
objective: Predict what an entangled partner will show, and explain why entanglement can't carry messages.

hook.prompt: Two particles are made together, then carried a kilometre apart. You measure one. Could that tell you, with certainty, what the other will show?

options.text: Yes, with certainty
No, a kilometre apart they can't be connected
options.feedback: Surprisingly, distance doesn't break this kind of link.

options.text: Only a rough guess, never certainty
options.feedback: For the right kind of pair, it's not a guess: it works every time.

hook.explanation: For entangled pairs, yes, every time and at any distance. The puzzle is how, when each result on its own looks random.

bricks.title: Two particles, one shared state
bricks.body: Particles are **entangled** when they share one joint state instead of each having its own. Take two electrons with linked **spin**, a property that always measures as either *up* or *down*. Each result on its own is a coin flip: 50/50. Yet whenever both are measured the same way, they come out **opposite**: one up, one down, every time, however far apart they are.

term.definition: A link between particles that makes their measurement results connected, even when they're far apart.

visual.html:
RunElectron AElectron B
1↑ Up↓ Down
2↓ Down↑ Up
3↓ Down↑ Up
4↑ Up↓ Down
visual.alt: A table of four runs: electron A's result is random, and electron B always shows the opposite.

bricks.prompt: Alice and Bob each hold one electron from a pair like this. Alice measures hers and gets *down*. Bob measures his the same way. What does he get?

options.text: Up
Down
options.feedback: That would be a matching result, but this pair always comes out opposite.

options.text: Up or down, 50/50
options.feedback: On its own each result is a coin flip, but once Alice's is known, Bob's is fixed: the opposite.

bricks.hint: This pair's results are always opposite when measured the same way.
bricks.explanation: Alice got down, and this pair always comes out opposite, so Bob's electron shows up.

bricks.prompt: Before anyone measures anything, what can you say about Alice's electron on its own?

options.text: It's equally likely to come out up or down
It will come out up, because it's entangled
options.feedback: Entanglement links the two results; it doesn't favour up or down for either one.

options.text: It will come out down, the opposite of Bob's
options.feedback: It will be opposite to Bob's, but Bob's isn't known yet either, so neither result is.

bricks.hint: Look at one electron's column in the table by itself.
bricks.explanation: Each electron alone is a coin flip. Only the pair is certain: whatever one shows, the other shows the opposite.

bricks.prompt: A lab measures pairs like these the same way each time. Tap the run that shows something went wrong.

visual.html:
RunElectron AElectron B
1↑ Up↓ Down
2↓ Down↑ Up
3↑ Up↑ Up
4↓ Down↑ Up

bricks.hint: Find the run where the two results aren't opposite.
bricks.explanation: In run 3 both electrons show up. Measured the same way, this pair should always come out opposite.

bricks.title: Not just a pair of gloves
bricks.body: Maybe the pair is like **gloves** split into two boxes: open one, find a left, and the other must be right. The answers were packed from the start. Gloves explain opposite results when both sides measure the same way. But physicists also measured at *different angles*. In these **Bell tests**, the results were linked more strongly than any pre-set answers could allow. So the particles don't simply carry hidden answers.

term.definition: An experiment that checks whether answers packed in advance could explain entangled results. They can't.

visual.html:
Gloves

Same check: always opposite ✓

Different angles: fails ✗

Entangled pair

Same check: always opposite ✓

Different angles: matches experiments ✓
visual.alt: Two cards: gloves explain the same-direction results but fail at different angles; entanglement explains both.

bricks.prompt: Which observation rules out the glove explanation?

options.text: Measured the same way, the results are always opposite
options.feedback: Gloves do that too: a left in one box always means a right in the other.

options.text: Measured at different angles, the results are linked more strongly than pre-set answers allow
Each result on its own is 50/50
options.feedback: Randomly packed gloves are 50/50 too: each box is equally likely to hold a left or a right.

bricks.hint: Which result could gloves not produce, however you packed them?
bricks.explanation: Gloves can copy the same-direction results. Only the different-angle comparison in Bell tests shows a link no pre-set answers can match.

bricks.prompt: A friend says: “Entanglement is just like gloves. Each particle knew its answer all along.” What did Bell tests find?

options.text: Pre-set answers can't produce the results seen in experiments
They confirmed it: the answers were set when the pair was made
options.feedback: That's the glove idea, and it's the one Bell tests ruled out.

options.text: They found the gloves picture works if you measure carefully enough
options.feedback: Care wasn't the issue: at different angles, no packing of answers matches the results.

bricks.hint: What did measuring at different angles show?
bricks.explanation: Your friend describes pre-set answers. Bell tests found entangled results are linked more strongly than any such answers allow.

bricks.title: Linked, but no messages
bricks.body: If measuring here fixes the result there, can Alice signal Bob instantly? **No.** Alice can't choose her result: it's a coin flip. So Bob sees a random string of ups and downs, whatever Alice does. The link only shows up when they **compare lists**, and that comparison travels by phone, radio, or post, never faster than light.

visual.html:
Alice's list

↑ ↓ ↓ ↑ ↓ ↑

Bob's list

↓ ↑ ↑ ↓ ↑ ↓

Each list alone looks random. Side by side, every pair is opposite.
visual.alt: Alice's and Bob's lists of results: each looks random on its own, but side by side every pair is opposite.

bricks.prompt: Alice wants to send Bob “yes” by making her electron come out up. Why doesn't this work?

options.text: She can't choose her result, so Bob's results stay random to him
The link breaks once the electrons are far apart
options.feedback: Distance doesn't break the link: the results stay opposite however far apart they are.

options.text: It works, but the message only travels at the speed of light
options.feedback: Speed isn't the problem. Alice can't pick her result, so there's no message to send.

bricks.hint: Can Alice decide what her measurement shows?
bricks.explanation: Alice's result is a coin flip she can't control, so nothing she does changes what Bob sees on his own.

bricks.prompt: Bob looks only at his own list of results, without Alice's. What does he see?

options.text: A random mix of up and down
All downs, because Alice got ups
options.feedback: Alice's results are a random mix, so Bob's opposite results are a random mix too.

options.text: A pattern that reveals what Alice measured
options.feedback: The pattern only appears when his list sits side by side with Alice's.

bricks.hint: What does one list look like on its own?
bricks.explanation: Each list alone is random. Bob only sees the link after Alice's list reaches him by ordinary means.

challenge.prompt: What's your verdict on the pitch?
challenge.situation: A startup asks you to invest: “We keep one electron of each entangled pair on Earth and send the other to Mars. Measuring on Earth sends messages to Mars instantly.”

options.text: Pass: Earth can't choose its results, so Mars sees only random ones until the lists arrive by radio
options.outcome: You keep your money. The pairs really are linked, but the link only shows when lists are compared by ordinary means.

options.text: Pass: the link would fade over the distance to Mars
options.outcome: Right call, wrong reason. Distance doesn't break the link; what fails is that nobody can choose their result.

options.text: Pass: entanglement is really just pre-set answers, like gloves
options.outcome: Right call, wrong reason. Bell tests ruled out pre-set answers. The real problem is that each result is random.

options.text: Invest: measuring one electron fixes the other, so messages arrive instantly
options.outcome: The product never works. Mars sees random ups and downs, with no message in them.

challenge.hint: Think about what Mars sees before any list arrives from Earth.
challenge.explanation: The results are linked at any distance, but each side's results are random, so no message can travel through the link.

takeaways: Entangled particles share one state: each result alone is random, but the pair's results are linked.
Pre-set answers, like gloves in boxes, can't explain the link; Bell tests ruled them out.
Entanglement can't send messages: the link only shows when results are compared by ordinary means.
